prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought optical timekeeping to the 1e-18 level and opened clock comparisons that test relativity and many-body physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock (B027) to Katori and Ye. I have gone back over the round-1 exchange to see whether anything should move me, and the weight of it supports the position rather than weakening it. The criterion I apply is the one I try to apply to every file: an original experiment or invention, verified by others, with the people credited being those who did the original work. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and his first strontium lattice demonstration are the invention. Ye's group then demonstrated that the concept works at about 1e-18 and used it to see many-body effects in the lattice. Independent clocks at several national laboratories have compared and reproduced these results, so verification does not depend on one group. This is also the entry on which members with different backgrounds converge, and the chair's summary shows that the doubts about it are about novelty relative to earlier prizes and about timing, not about whether the science is true. I take the point made by Danielsson and Kroll that the citation must say what the precision has actually shown, and I have changed my citation wording accordingly: it now names the magic-wavelength trap and the 1e-18 level, and also the tests of relativity and the many-body physics that clock comparisons have already delivered, rather than leaning on promised applications such as geodesy or dark-matter searches. On the chair's question about waiting for the redefinition of the second: I would not wait. The prize is for the invention and its verified performance, not for a metrological decision taken by another body, and waiting costs us nothing scientifically but gains nothing either.
statement.case_against: I do not want to soften the objections. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, Haroche) cover neighbouring ground, and Ye in particular worked with comb-stabilised lasers and cavity stabilisation; if the citation reads as better clocks after 2005 and 2012, it will look like a third prize for one programme. The answer I find sound is that the magic-wavelength lattice, with many atoms interrogated at once, is a different mechanism that reached a different regime of precision, but that answer works only if the citation is specific. Second, the fundamental results so far are bounds and redshift tests, not a surprise from nature, and Danielsson and Lindroth are right to say so. Third, the credit is defensible but not airtight: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and Derevianko did important work, and Ye's role is closer to decisive development than to the original idea. A prize for the invention and development of an instrument is exactly the kind I would resist if it were only a more elegant version of someone else's experiment, so I rely on Katori's priority to carry the part. Finally, giving up B053, where I know the instruments best, remains a real cost, and I still cannot settle the Krivanek question from what is in front of me.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B057 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as first choice, answers the 2016 overlap by distinguishing topological phases in model systems from Z2 band topology in real materials, and says he would move the clock to the top rather than force an unsettled B057 if the credit question is not resolved.
responses.response: Your answer on 2016 is a good one, and I accept that B057 is a distinct discovery and not a repeat of Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz. The Kane-Mele proposal in 2005 and the Konig-Molenkamp measurement in 2007 are unambiguous milestones. My difficulty is the one you name yourself. Between those two sits the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction that told experimentalists which material and which thickness to use, and I cannot be absolutely sure we would be crediting those who did the original work if that step is outside the names. Zhang's death makes the omission permanent, and a citation worded around the Z2 concept and the first observation would still have to explain the gap. You also say you would move to the clock if the credit stays unsettled. I take that as the most honest statement in the round-1 file, and I ask you to tell us in round 2 whether you think the credit can be defended, since that is the evidence that would change my view. I keep B057 as my first alternative because the science is sound and I do not think it is overruled by the 2016 prize.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B027 first because the magic-wavelength condition, a cancellation of light shifts, is itself the discovery, and she argues the 2005 and 2012 prizes made the clock possible without covering neutral atoms trapped in a lattice; she notes that her atomic-theory background may make the case seem more natural to her.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the mechanism, and I accept your caution about your own background; I find the case persuasive from a quite different background, that of the experimentalist who asks what was actually built and measured. Your statement that Zoller should not be added is sensible, since it would blur a pair that is clean and would double count him against B060 and B006. I would still ask you, as the member who knows the atomic structure best, to say whether Ye's contribution on the many-body side, such as spin-exchange and the SU(N) clock physics, is distinct from Katori's magic-wavelength idea and necessary to the citation. If it is, the two-name credit is well founded and the words invention and development are accurate. If it is not, we should ask whether Ye is credited for precision alone, which is the weaker claim and one I would want to state openly in the citation.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B027 and wants the citation to rest on what the precision has shown, such as millimetre-scale redshift tests and many-body clock physics, and not on better clocks; he also argues against B053 as an instrument whose results lie mostly in materials science.
responses.response: I accept your wording point and have rewritten the citation to say what the clocks have shown, not only what they can do. On B053 I disagree in part. I do not think an instrument that broke the sub-angstrom limit is only materials science, because it let us see atoms and interfaces that physics could not previously resolve, but I accept that this is a judgement the committee has not settled and that my own interest shows. I was moved by your second point, that the attribution problem for the corrected microscope, namely Krivanek, is a stronger reason than the physics-or-materials question to hold B053 for another year. You also suggest IceCube (B041) as an alternative. I would be interested in how you would answer the objection that the discovery paper credits a roughly three-hundred-person collaboration, since that is the same principle that makes me uneasy about naming three people for the Higgs entry.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B027 first, wants the citation to rest on demonstrated accuracy and comparisons, notes that B053 has only two ranks and carries a credit dispute that B027 does not, and asks whether aberration-corrected TEM is physics or materials instrumentation.
responses.response: We agree on the substance, and your caution that geodesy and dark-matter searches are promises rather than results is built into my new citation. On your question, I would say aberration-corrected TEM is physics in the sense that the limit was set by wave optics and electron-lens aberrations, but the tool's scientific yield is mostly in materials, and that is a fair reason for the Physics committee to hesitate; it is not a reason for me to claim the opposite. I also accept your point that a verified 1e-18 agreement between independent clocks is a stronger basis than image quality. You asked whether I know a third name with an original experiment for B027. I do not from what is before me; Takamoto's 2005 demonstration of a strontium lattice clock is a real contribution, but it followed Katori's proposal and was made in Katori's group, so I read it as part of Katori's priority and not as a separate claim.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B057 and says that a clean credit is no reason to prefer a pair, but regards B027 as a legitimate winner against which he cannot make a scientific case, and he asks whether the citation can be framed without implying that the HgTe prediction is unrecognised.
responses.response: I agree that a small number of people on a technique is not by itself a virtue, and the prize should not go to the pair merely because it is tidy. What recommends B027 to me is that the original proposal, the first demonstration and the verification of the performance all sit with identifiable people and have been confirmed by others. For B057 I would put the question you asked Eriksson to him again in a sharper form: if the citation names only the Z2 classification and the HgTe observation, is it true to the historical record, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang left unmentioned? I would like your view on that, since you and Eriksson are the two members who can judge it. I do not claim your position is wrong. I am saying that for me, until that point is resolved, the attribution gap outweighs the novelty argument.

uncertainties: Whether Ye's contribution is distinct invention (many-body and spin-exchange clock physics, the first demonstrations at the highest precision) or decisive development of Katori's concept, and whether the citation needs to say so; I have kept the words invention and development to reflect both.

Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes overlap enough with the lattice clock for the committee to judge it as a third prize for one programme; my answer depends on the citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice specifically.

Whether the credit for B057 can be defended without Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; I cannot judge priority in band-topology as Eriksson and Mehlig can and I am working from memory on the sequence 2005, 2006, 2007.
For B053, whether Krivanek's corrected-STEM work is an independent original contribution that would have to be credited; I cannot settle this from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: No specific personal or institutional conflict applies to B027, the lattice clock, or to B057; I have no connection to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. For B053 I repeat my disclosure: spherical-aberration correction is my own field of transmission electron microscopy, I am IFSM president, and my community overlaps with the corrector developers, although I have no co-authorship or institutional tie to Rose, Haider or Urban; I am now only an alternative on B053 and not a supporter of it as a lead. Johansson is a Chalmers colleague who works on circuit QED (B036), which is not in my configuration and I have no stake in it.
